title: Knee ligaments and menisci
claims: The ACL runs from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the medial side of the lateral femoral condyle and prevents anterior translation of the tibia on the femur.
The PCL runs from the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the lateral side of the medial femoral condyle and prevents posterior translation of the tibia.
The MCL (tibial collateral ligament) resists valgus stress; the LCL (fibular collateral ligament) resists varus stress.
The medial meniscus is C-shaped and attached to the joint capsule and deep MCL, so it is less mobile and injured more often than the more circular lateral meniscus.

The unhappy (O'Donoghue) triad is classically ACL + MCL + medial meniscus injury from a lateral blow to a planted, flexed knee (valgus with rotation); acute studies find the lateral meniscus torn more often.
ACL tear: a pop, rapid haemarthrosis and instability; Lachman test (most sensitive) and anterior drawer show increased anterior tibial translation.
MCL tear: medial pain and laxity on valgus stress at 30 degrees of flexion.
Meniscal tear: joint-line tenderness, locking or catching; McMurray test. MRI is the imaging test of choice for ligament and meniscal tears.
PCL tear: a posterior force on the proximal tibia with the knee flexed (dashboard injury, fall on the flexed knee); posterior drawer test and posterior sag sign.
